title: Failure and recovery: a request with no timeout hangs a script
summary: One slow API stalls a whole job.

steps.n: A nightly script calls an API with the requests library and finishes in seconds.
The API stops answering and keeps the connection open without sending data.
The call has no timeout, so it waits and the script never reaches its next line.
The scheduler reports the job still running hours later and the next run is skipped or overlaps.
Stack dump or py-spy shows the thread blocked in a socket read inside the client.
Set a connect and read timeout on every call and catch the timeout error.
Retry with a small backoff and a limit, then fail clearly with a message and a non-zero exit code.
The scheduler shows the job ending within its time limit even when the API is down.

title: Failure and recovery: the wrong Python environment breaks a deploy
summary: Works on my machine, fails on the server.

steps.n: The script runs fine on a laptop where the packages were installed globally over time.
The script is copied to a server without a lock file or a recorded list of packages.
The server reports a missing module, and after installing it, a newer version behaves differently.
The job fails with ModuleNotFoundError, then with a changed function signature.
pip freeze on both machines shows different versions and which python is used is not the same.
Create a virtualenv, pin versions in a requirements file with hashes, and install from it.
The deploy step creates the environment from the lock file, so every machine is the same.
A fresh server runs the script with the same versions and the same results.

title: Failure and recovery: a stale DNS answer sends traffic to the old server
summary: Cached records outlive a cutover.

steps.n: A client asks a resolver for the service name and receives an address with a long time to live.
The team moves the service to a new address and updates the record at the authoritative server.
The resolver keeps serving the old answer until the cached time to live runs out.
Some users reach the old server, which is draining, and see errors while others work fine.
dig shows different answers from different resolvers and the remaining time to live in each.
Wait for the time to live, or flush the caches you control, and keep the old server serving until then.
Lower the time to live a day before a planned cutover and raise it again afterwards.
dig from several resolvers returns the new address and the old server sees no more traffic.

title: Failure and recovery: a smaller path MTU drops large packets
summary: Small requests work, large ones hang.

steps.n: Packets of 1500 bytes travel from client to server over ordinary links.
A VPN tunnel is added on the path and its overhead lowers the usable packet size to about 1400 bytes.
A large packet with the do not fragment bit cannot fit and the router drops it, but the message back is blocked.
Pings and small requests work, but a large download or a TLS handshake stalls and times out.
ping with a set size and the do not fragment flag finds the largest size that passes.
Lower the MTU on the tunnel interface or clamp the segment size so packets fit.
Permit the needed ICMP messages so path discovery can work for other traffic.
Large transfers complete at normal speed and the handshake no longer hangs.

title: Failure and recovery: a container restarts in a loop
summary: The exit code points at the cause.

steps.n: The orchestrator starts a new container from the latest image tag.
The main process exits right after start with a non-zero exit code.
The restart policy starts it again and again, with a growing delay between attempts.
The status shows restarting or crash loop and the service is never ready.
docker logs shows a missing environment variable that the new image now requires.
Code 1 points at the application and 137 would point at memory limits being hit.
Provide the variable or roll back to the previous image tag that worked.
The container stays running, passes its health check, and the restart count stops increasing.

title: Failure and recovery: an image pull hits the registry rate limit
summary: Builds stall on a public registry.

steps.n: The pipeline pulls base images from a public registry without logging in.
A busy day produces many builds from the same shared address.
The registry returns too many requests and refuses further pulls for a few hours.
Builds fail at the pull step with a rate limit message, even though the code did not change.
The response headers show the remaining pulls and the time when the limit resets.
Log in with a registry account to raise the limit, or retry after the reset.
Mirror the needed base images into a private registry or pull through a cache.
Builds pull from the private registry and no longer depend on the public limit.

title: Failure and recovery: a bad release is caught by a canary
summary: Small blast radius, fast rollback.

steps.n: The pipeline builds the release and all tests pass, so it is approved for production.
Only five percent of traffic is routed to the new version while ninety five stays on the old one.
The canary reports errors and latency, and monitoring compares them with the old version.
The canary error rate is ten times higher than the baseline for three minutes in a row.
The pipeline stops the rollout and sends all traffic back to the old version without waiting for a person.
The operator reads the canary logs and finds a missing database column the new code expects.
A migration is added and tested, and a new release is built.
The next canary stays within thresholds, so the rollout moves from five percent to fifty and then to everyone.

title: Failure and recovery: a flaky test erodes trust in the pipeline
summary: Retries hide the problem, quarantine fixes it.

steps.n: The pipeline passes on most runs and developers merge without thinking about it.
One test fails about one run in ten with a timing error that has nothing to do with the change.
Developers press the rerun button until it passes and stop reading the failures.
Each rerun adds ten minutes, and a real failure is dismissed as just the flaky one.
A report of pass and fail by test over the last fifty runs shows which test is flaky.
The flaky test is moved to a separate non-blocking job with an owner and a due date.
The test waits for a condition instead of a fixed sleep, and its shared state is isolated.
The test returns to the blocking set and the failure rate is tracked to stay at zero.

title: Failure and recovery: a pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff
summary: Read the events and the previous logs.

steps.n: A deployment rollout creates new pods with a changed config map reference.
The container starts, the application exits with an error, and the kubelet records the exit code.
The kubelet restarts the container with growing delays, and the status becomes CrashLoopBackOff.
kubectl get pods shows a growing restart count and the pod never becomes ready.
kubectl describe pod shows the last state, the exit code and events about back-off restarting.
kubectl logs with the previous flag shows the application complaining about a missing config key.
Correct the config map key, apply it, and roll the deployment so the pods pick it up.
Pods become ready, the restart count stays at zero, and the rollout reports successfully rolled out.

title: Failure and recovery: a Service has no endpoints
summary: Selectors and labels must match.

steps.n: A Service selects pods by the label app equals web and traffic reaches them.
A change renames the pod label to app equals website but leaves the Service selector unchanged.
The Service now matches zero pods, so its list of endpoints becomes empty.
Clients get connection refused or timeouts even though every pod is running and ready.
kubectl get endpoints shows none for the Service, which points at the selector.
kubectl get pods with show-labels and the Service selector show different values.
Make the selector and pod labels match, and prefer one shared label set in a single template.
Endpoints list the pod addresses and requests reach the pods again.

title: Failure and recovery: etcd loses quorum
summary: Restore from a snapshot, then bring members back.

steps.n: Three etcd members agree on every write and the API server answers quickly.
Two of three members are lost together when a rack fails, and quorum needs two.
The API server cannot write, so kubectl commands time out and no new pods can be scheduled.
Existing pods keep running, but nothing changes, and the API server logs say etcd is unavailable.
The operator finds the latest snapshot and checks its date and size.
A snapshot is restored into a new data directory and a fresh cluster of members is started from it.
The API servers point at the restored members and nodes reconnect.
kubectl shows the expected objects, the member list is healthy, and a new snapshot is taken.

title: Failure and recovery: an upgrade breaks workloads
summary: Remove deprecated APIs before upgrading.

steps.n: The operator reads the release notes and plans a minor version upgrade, one version at a time.
The control plane is upgraded first and starts serving the newer API version.
A manifest uses an API version that was removed, so applying it now returns an error.
A deployment pipeline fails to apply, and a controller using the old API stops reconciling.
A scan of the manifests and the API server metrics lists clients still calling deprecated APIs.
Update the manifests to the supported API version and redeploy the affected workloads.
Nodes are drained and upgraded one at a time, with the drain respecting disruption budgets.
All nodes report the new version and every workload is ready.

title: Failure and recovery: a stuck state lock blocks every plan
summary: Unlock safely, only when no run is active.

steps.n: Terraform locks the remote state, plans, applies, and releases the lock.
The apply is interrupted when the runner is killed, so the lock is never released.
An engineer runs plan and sees an error that the state is locked by another operation.
The lock info shows a run id and a time, and the pipeline shows no active run.
The engineer checks that no apply is really running before touching the lock.
terraform force-unlock with the lock id releases it, and the person records why it was done.
A new plan shows whether the interrupted apply left a partial change to review.
Add a timeout and retries to the runner and keep applies in one serialised pipeline job.

title: Failure and recovery: a manual change causes drift
summary: Plan finds it and code decides what is right.

steps.n: The code, the state and the real resources all agree and the plan shows no changes.
During an incident someone widens a security group rule in the console.
The real resource now differs from the state and from the code.
A nightly plan reports one change that would remove the new rule.
The team asks whether the manual change should stay or be removed.
If it should stay, update the code so it matches and run the plan to confirm no changes.
If not, apply to restore the declared value, and note it in the incident record.
Restrict console edits and run the drift plan on a schedule with alerts.

title: Failure and recovery: a region outage and a failover
summary: Rehearsed failover turns a disaster into a drill.

steps.n: Traffic goes through DNS to the primary region and the standby receives replicated data.
A power and network failure makes the primary region unavailable to users.
Health checks from outside the region fail three times in a row.
DNS answers change to the standby region, or a traffic manager moves users, within the record's time to live.
The standby database is promoted and the application config points at it.
New requests succeed in the standby region after a short interruption.
When the primary is healthy again, data is synced back before traffic is moved in a quiet window.
The measured recovery time is compared with the target and the runbook is updated.

title: Failure and recovery: an unexpected cloud bill
summary: Budgets and tags find the owner fast.

steps.n: Daily spend follows the usual pattern and stays below the monthly budget line.
A test job leaves a large cluster running and a log bucket with no lifecycle rule grows daily.
A budget alert fires at eighty percent of the month on day twelve.
The cost report grouped by tag and service shows one project accounting for most of the rise.
The tag points at the owner who confirms the cluster is not needed.
The cluster is deleted and the bucket gets an expiry rule for old data.
Tags become mandatory, budgets get alerts per team, and idle resources are reported weekly.
Daily spend returns to the normal line the next day.

title: Failure and recovery: debugging an AccessDenied error
summary: Work out which layer said no.

steps.n: A deployment role calls an action on a storage bucket and the call returns AccessDenied.
The engineer checks that the role's own policy allows the action on that exact resource.
The bucket policy has an explicit deny for requests that do not come through the private endpoint.
A permissions boundary or an organisation policy can also remove permissions, so they are checked too.
The decision log shows an explicit deny in the bucket policy, and an explicit deny always wins.
Route the call through the private endpoint, or update the policy condition for this role.
The same call now succeeds, and the change is made in code, not in the console.
The fix adds one condition and no wildcard, and the access review notes it.

title: Failure and recovery: a leaked access key
summary: Revoke first, investigate second.

steps.n: A long-lived access key is pushed into a public repository by mistake.
Within minutes, a bot uses the key to start large instances in many regions.
A usage anomaly alert and the audit log show unusual calls from an unknown address.
The security team deactivates the key at once, before anything else is done.
The audit log lists every call made with that key and the resources created.
Unwanted resources are deleted, and any new credentials created by the attacker are removed.
The workload moves to short-lived role credentials so there is no long-lived key to leak.
Secret scanning, least-privilege roles and cost alerts shorten the time to notice next time.

title: Failure and recovery: an alert storm buries the real problem
summary: Group and route so one cause is one page.

steps.n: A database slows down and fifty services that depend on it start timing out.
Each service fires its own alert and the on-call phone receives fifty pages in two minutes.
The responder cannot tell which alert is the cause and which are the effects.
Alerts are grouped by cluster and dependency so a single message shows the common cause.
A rule suppresses the downstream alerts while the database alert is firing.
The dashboard for the database shows slow queries and connection saturation.
Raise the pool and kill the long query, and services recover without any change to the services.
Alerts resolve in order, the page count is one, and the rules are kept for the next time.

title: Failure and recovery: high cardinality crashes the metrics server
summary: One label can create millions of series.

steps.n: A request counter carries labels for method and status code, giving a few dozen series.
A change adds the user id as a label so that debugging a single user is easier.
Every user becomes a new series, and memory use climbs with each scrape.
Dashboards slow down, queries time out, and the server is killed for running out of memory.
A query for the series count by metric name shows one metric with millions of series.
The label is dropped in code and relabelling drops it at scrape time right away.
Per-user data goes to logs or traces, which are built for high cardinality.
A limit on series per target and a review check on new labels stop it next time.

title: Failure and recovery: the error budget runs out
summary: Reliability work takes priority.

steps.n: A ninety nine point nine percent target gives the service forty three minutes of errors per month.
A release causes errors for thirty minutes and a second incident adds fifteen more.
The tracker shows the monthly budget fully used on day nineteen, with eleven days still to go.
The agreed policy says feature releases pause and reliability work comes first until the budget recovers.
The SRE and product team list the causes and choose the fixes that remove the most risk.
Add a canary step, a rollback test, and a timeout fix for the slow dependency.
Releases restart when the rolling window shows budget back, with the new checks in place.
The next month ends with budget left and fewer pages.

title: Failure and recovery: a bad change during an incident
summary: Recent changes are the first suspect.

steps.n: Error rates rise at 10:02 and the responder starts an incident.
The incident lead assigns a responder, a communicator and a note taker.
The change log shows a config rollout at 10:00 to the same service.
The rollout is the leading suspect because the timing and the affected service match.
Roll back the config first, since a rollback is quicker and safer than diagnosing under pressure.
Error rates fall within three minutes, which confirms the hypothesis.
The team writes down the timeline, and the cause is found later in calm conditions.
Staged rollouts and an automatic rollback on error spikes become action items.

title: Failure and recovery: ransomware and a clean restore
summary: Immutable backups decide the outcome.

steps.n: A stolen password for a remote access account gives the attacker a way into the network.
The attacker moves between servers and gains an administrator account.
The attacker tries to delete backups, but the immutable copies cannot be changed before their retention date.
Files are encrypted and a ransom note appears on the servers.
The response team isolates affected network segments and disables the stolen accounts.
Clean systems are rebuilt from known good images and data is restored from the immutable backup.
Multi-factor authentication, network segmentation and tested restore times are put in place.
The timeline and gaps become action items, and the restore time is compared with the target.

title: Failure and recovery: a critical vulnerability is announced
summary: Know where it runs, then patch by priority.

steps.n: A critical flaw is announced in a widely used library, with a fix released the same day.
The software inventory lists every service and image that includes the vulnerable version.
Internet-facing services go first, then internal ones, and unused images are removed.
The dependency is updated and the pipeline rebuilds and tests each affected service.
Fixed versions are rolled out in stages, with the same checks as any release.
A rescan shows no remaining vulnerable versions in running workloads.
The team records what was affected, when it was fixed and what monitoring watched meanwhile.
An automatic dependency update and a scan on every build cut the time next time.

title: Failure and recovery: a playbook fails halfway across a fleet
summary: Idempotent tasks make re-running safe.

steps.n: The operator runs a playbook that updates the configuration on twenty web servers.
Without a batch limit, all hosts restart their service at nearly the same moment.
A template contains a typo, and the service fails to start on every host that applied it.
The load balancer sees every back end as unhealthy and the site is down.
The operator stops the play and uses the previous config from version control to restore service.
Correct the template, run a syntax check, and use check mode with diff before applying.
Idempotent tasks skip hosts that are already correct and only change what is still wrong.
Use serial batches and a failure threshold so one bad host stops the run early.

title: Failure and recovery: a lost Vault password
summary: Plan secret recovery before you need it.

steps.n: Secrets for the playbooks are stored in an encrypted vault file.
The one engineer who knew the vault password leaves and the password was only on their laptop.
The playbook cannot decrypt the file and every deploy fails with a decryption error.
The team checks the secret store and the pipeline for a stored copy of the password.
If a copy exists, it is used to re-key the vault with a new password stored in the secret store.
If none exists, every secret in the file must be rotated at its source and the file recreated.
The password is held in the shared secret manager with two named owners and an access log.
A fresh clone of the repository decrypts and runs in the pipeline using the stored password.

title: Failure and recovery: replica lag serves stale data
summary: Reads from a replica can be behind.

steps.n: The application writes to the primary and reads from a replica a few milliseconds behind.
A bulk update runs on the primary and produces a large amount of change data quickly.
The replica applies changes more slowly and falls minutes behind.
Users save a change and then see the old value, and support calls say it did not save.
The replica lag metric and replication status show the delay and the slow apply thread.
Send reads that must see the latest write to the primary and pause the bulk job.
Break the job into small batches and give the replica more resources for applying changes.
Lag stays under a second during the next bulk job and read-your-write cases work.

title: Failure and recovery: a long transaction blocks the table
summary: One idle transaction can stall writers.

steps.n: A tool opens a transaction, updates a row and then sits idle without committing.
The row lock stays held for as long as the transaction is open.
Another session tries to update the same row and waits in the lock queue.
More sessions queue behind it and the connection pool fills with waiting requests.
The DBA queries the lock views and finds the idle transaction at the head of the chain.
The blocking session is ended, which rolls it back and releases the lock.
Set an idle in transaction timeout and make the tool commit or roll back promptly.
The queue clears, requests complete, and the lock wait graph is empty.

title: Failure and recovery: a goroutine leak grows memory
summary: Every goroutine needs a way to stop.

steps.n: Each request starts a goroutine that sends its result on an unbuffered channel.
The handler times out and returns before it reads from the channel.
The goroutine waits to send and nothing will ever receive, so it never exits.
Memory and the goroutine count climb with every timed-out request until the pod is killed.
A goroutine profile shows thousands stuck at the same channel send line.
Pass a context, use a buffered channel or select on the context so the goroutine can stop.
A test checks that the goroutine count returns to its starting value after a timeout.
The goroutine count stays flat under load and the pod no longer restarts.

title: Failure and recovery: a nil map write panics a service
summary: A panic should not take down everything.

steps.n: A handler builds a response using a map declared with var and never created.
The handler writes a key to the nil map, and Go raises a panic.
With no recovery, the panic ends the whole process and every in-flight request fails.
The service restarts, and the logs show a stack trace pointing at the map assignment.
The stack trace names the file and line, and the map was never initialised with make.
Create the map with make before writing to it, or return an error when input is missing.
A recover in middleware turns an unexpected panic into a 500 response and a logged stack.
A test with empty input passes, and the service stays up under the same request.

title: Failure and recovery: a failed Helm upgrade and rollback
summary: The release history is your safety net.

steps.n: The operator runs helm upgrade with a new image tag and a changed values file.
Helm renders the templates and applies the changes, and the new pods fail their readiness probe.
The release is marked failed and the old pods are still serving because of the rolling update.
helm status and helm history show the failed revision and the last good revision.
kubectl describe on the pods shows the readiness probe path changed in the new chart version.
helm rollback to the last good revision restores the previous manifests as a new revision.
Correct the probe path, test with helm template and a dry run, then upgrade again.
Use atomic with a timeout so a failed upgrade rolls back automatically.

title: Failure and recovery: a values typo is silently ignored
summary: Schema validation catches mistakes early.

steps.n: The engineer sets replicaCont instead of replicaCount in the production values file.
The chart does not know that key, so it ignores it and uses the default of one replica.
The release succeeds, so there is no error message to warn anyone.
Under load the service has one pod and falls over, while the values file looks right.
helm get values and helm template show the rendered replica count is one.
Correct the key, and add a values schema file so unknown keys fail at install time.
A diff check between rendered environments is added to the pipeline.
The release shows the expected replicas and a bad key now fails with a clear message.

title: Failure and recovery: Argo CD syncs and then flips back
summary: Two controllers fight over one field.

steps.n: The repository says replicas is two and Argo CD syncs it to the cluster.
The horizontal autoscaler changes replicas to five because of load.
Argo CD compares and marks the application OutOfSync because replicas differs.
With self-heal on, Argo CD sets replicas back to two and the autoscaler sets it to five again.
The application flips between the two states and the history fills with syncs.
The diff shows only the replicas field, which points at two owners for one field.
Remove replicas from the manifest, or tell Argo CD to ignore that field in the application.
The application stays Synced and Healthy while the autoscaler changes the count.

title: Failure and recovery: a bad commit reaches the cluster
summary: Revert in the repository, not in the cluster.

steps.n: A change with a wrong image tag is merged to the main branch of the config repository.
Argo CD sees the new commit and applies it to the cluster within minutes.
The pods cannot pull the image and the application becomes Degraded.
An alert shows the health status and the sync revision that caused it.
The developer reverts the commit in the repository, which keeps the history honest.
Argo CD syncs the reverted state and the old pods become the desired state again.
Pods run, the application shows Synced and Healthy, and traffic is normal.
A required review and a preview environment catch a bad tag before it is merged.

title: Failure and recovery: the prompt overflows the context window
summary: Long input is cut or rejected.

steps.n: Early conversations fit easily in the model context window and answers are accurate.
A long conversation with pasted documents grows past the window limit.
The application silently drops the oldest messages to make the request fit.
The model forgets earlier instructions and answers as if they were never given.
Logs of token counts show the request was trimmed and the system instructions were among the dropped parts.
Keep instructions pinned, summarise older turns, and retrieve only the relevant document parts.
Count tokens before sending and warn or compact when the request nears the limit.
A long conversation test keeps following the original instructions to the end.

title: Failure and recovery: a confident wrong answer
summary: Ground answers in sources and check them.

steps.n: A user asks about an internal policy that the model was never trained on.
The application sends the question without any policy text.
The model produces a fluent, specific answer that is not true.
The user follows the wrong guidance, and the error is only noticed later.
Reviewing the prompt shows there was no source text, so the answer could not have been grounded.
Retrieve the relevant policy passages and instruct the model to answer only from them and to say when unsure.
The answer cites the passages so a user can check them.
A test set of questions with known answers measures how often the system now cites correctly.

title: Failure and recovery: the model stops returning valid JSON
summary: Validate, repair, and retry.

steps.n: A prompt asks for JSON and the model has returned valid JSON in every test.
The model adds a short sentence before the JSON on some responses.
The application's JSON parser fails and the request returns a server error.
An error rate of a few percent appears with no code change on the application side.
Logged raw outputs show the extra text and a trailing comma in a few cases.
Use structured output with a schema, validate every response, and retry once with the error message.
If it still fails, return a clear error or a safe default and log the sample.
The error rate returns to near zero, and failures are visible in a dashboard.

title: Failure and recovery: a prompt edit breaks a working case
summary: Test prompts like code.

steps.n: An author rewrites a prompt to fix one complaint and sees that example improve.
There is no test set, so no one checks the other twenty common cases.
The new prompt goes live and handles the complaint well.
A week later, support finds that refund requests are now answered in the wrong format.
Prompt version history shows the edit and the date that matches the first bad answer.
Revert to the previous version and build a test set from real cases that includes the complaint.
Every prompt change runs the test set and the reviewer sees what got better and what got worse.
The next edit passes all cases, with the previous failure now a permanent test.

title: Failure and recovery: a skill never triggers
summary: The description decides when it loads.

steps.n: A user asks for a task that the skill was written to handle.
Claude reads the skill descriptions and the description is vague, so it does not match the request.
Claude answers without the skill and the output ignores the team conventions.
The author expects the skill to run, yet the transcript shows it was never loaded.
Comparing the description with real requests shows missing words that users actually use.
Rewrite the description to say what it does and when to use it, with the trigger phrases.
Try ten phrasings, including ones that should not trigger, and record which load the skill.
The skill loads on the right requests and stays quiet on the others.

title: Failure and recovery: an overbroad skill triggers on everything
summary: Narrow scope and add a boundary.

steps.n: A skill for writing release notes is installed with a short generic description.
A user asks for a meeting summary and the skill loads anyway.
The skill's template makes the summary read like release notes.
Users complain that unrelated answers now follow a strange structure.
The description says documents and writing, which matches almost any request.
Narrow the description to release notes for software changes and add when not to use it.
Run requests that should and should not trigger and check each outcome.
Meeting summaries are normal again and release notes use the template.
